source.title: Scaling Wearable Foundation Models
source.authors: Girish Narayanswamy; Xin Liu; Kumar Ayush; Yu-Zhe Yang; X. Xu; Shun Liao; Jake Garrison; Shyam Tailor; Jacob E. Sunshine; Yun Liu; Tim Althoff; S. Narayanan; Pushmeet Kohli; Jie-Ning Zhan; Mark Malhotra; Shwetak N. Patel; Samy Abdel-Ghaffar; Daniel McDuff

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some text and table labels are visibly garbled, but the relevant scaling results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling in wearable sensor models, a different modality, and reports saturation at high data and compute scales that qualifies a simple power-law account. It does not test the language-model results directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps and downstream task measurements. Cited language, vision, and other scaling results are not recorded as rows. Values selected only as hyperparameters are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own data, model-size and compute sweeps on wearable sensor models. It reports held-out masked-reconstruction MSE, which is the pretraining objective, plus downstream accuracy. This tests power-law scaling in a new modality (V5) and saturation of the curve (V7). It is a new-setting result, not mainly an argument against a version, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors claim to establish scaling laws for wearable sensor models: loss follows a power law in compute, with an added constant for saturation, and data, model and compute scaling help generative and discriminative tasks. They note saturation near 10^7 hours and around 100M parameters. They attribute it to the masked pretext task, short 5-hour context and limited data diversity.
record.recipe_differences: This is an extension to wearable sensor time series, not a reproduction of language-model cross-entropy scaling. It uses masked reconstruction pretraining and held-out mean squared error, with data, model-size, and compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome changes with data volume and model size: gains diminish at the largest data scale, and the largest listed model performs worse than LSM-Base on interpolation and extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal total hours, fewer subjects with more hours per subject gives similar loss (Fig. 4a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling depends on total data volume more than on data-source diversity (subjects).

record.problems: The study concerns wearable sensor reconstruction, not language-model cross-entropy. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling results. The compute-scaling figure is not numerically tabulated in the text. The authors note saturation and identify potential limits in the pretraining task, dataset construction, and data diversity.
record.rows_left_out: Table 9 contains further model-by-data-scale combinations beyond the Base-model data sweep and the model-size sweep at 6.6 M hours; these were not extracted to keep the record within 60 rows. Table 10's linear-probe and convolutional-probe results were also omitted; fine-tuning results were retained as the downstream scaling measure.

untested.parts: Whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs; no extrapolation of fitted laws is reported.
Compute-optimal split of parameters and tokens. A Pareto front is shown, but no allocation exponents are reported.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count. Patch-size and masking ablations change the task setup, not model shape.
Image, video and audio modalities; repeated-data regimes; fitted exponents for the data and model sweeps.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; downstream scaling with model size or compute.
Dependence of exponents on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method; disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: Data-scaling curves across all four model sizes, showing that small models (Tiny) beat larger ones at small data (0.005M: 0.50 vs 0.67 MSE). This illustrates the data-bottleneck condition.
missing.locator: Table 9 rows for Tiny/Small/Large at 0.005–3.8M hours; Fig. 3

missing.what: Downstream data scaling under linear and convolutional probes, which is also non-monotonic at 6.6M (e.g., linear-probe exercise accuracy 88.0 to 84.7)
Larger models are more sample-efficient (test loss vs samples seen)

record.verdict_notes: The metric is held-out MSE on the same masked-reconstruction objective used in pretraining, so it is a pretraining loss, which makes it a valid V5 test. No uncertainty is reported and no fitted exponents are given. The 40M-hour set is subject-imbalanced, which confounds the saturation result. Table 9 does not hold model size fixed while varying data at optimal allocation, so the model-size reversals reflect a data bottleneck, as the authors say. V6 rows concern sensor models, not LMs; the link is kept on the reading that V6 is modality-general. The reader's V7 limits_scope label is removed, because untested parts belong under untested.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy scaling in language models; the study uses wearable sensor models and reconstruction error.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
A fixed-compute, loss-minimising allocation between parameter count and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities beyond wearable sensor data; repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; language-model tasks.
Dependence of fitted exponents on parameter counting, schedules, data, and fitting method; disagreement between published laws.

rows.subject: LSM
rows.operation_detail: Compute-scaling experiment; reconstruction performance plotted against compute.
rows.note: The authors describe a power-law trend over multiple orders of compute, but report saturation at the upper end and use an additive constant. No numeric plotted values are stated.
rows.check: The compute Pareto front is described as a power law, nearly linear on log-log over multiple orders, with saturation at the top, fitted as L=aC^b+c. Figure only; no fitted a, b, c values are stated. It should also be linked to V5.

relationships.condition: Wearable sensor masked-reconstruction pretraining, compute front and data/model sweeps up to about 10^6–10^7 hours and up to 110M parameters
relationships.reason: Test MSE falls with data (R1–R4, R7–R10, R13–R16) and with model size through Base (R19–R21, R23–R25, R27–R29). The compute front follows a power law plus a constant (R31).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE decreased with data and model size through Base, while the compute frontier followed a power law plus a constant.

relationships.condition: Data beyond about 3.8M hours and models larger than 110M at 6.6M hours
relationships.reason: There is no gain from 3.8M to 6.6M or 40M hours (R5, R6, R11, R12, R17, R18). The 328M model is equal to or worse than 110M (R22, R26, R30). The authors attribute this to the pretext task, data diversity and overfitting.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing data from 3.8M to 6.6M or 40M hours brought no gain, and the 328M model matched or underperformed 110M.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned exercise detection vs pretraining data size, sensor models
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises from 68.3 to 90.3 and mAP from 58.9 to 97.0, monotonically across 0.005M–6.6M hours (R32–R41).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy rises monotonically from 68.3 to 90.3 and mAP from 58.9 to 97.0 as pretraining data grows from 0.005M to 6.6M hours.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned activity recognition vs pretraining data size
relationships.reason: Gains up to 0.5M hours, then a dip at 3.8M and a flat result at 6.6M, so the trend is non-monotonic (R42–R51).
relationships.display_finding: Performance improved through 0.5M hours, dipped at 3.8M hours and was flat at 6.6M hours.

relationships.condition: Upper end of compute and data ranges in sensor models
relationships.reason: The curve saturates and needs an additive constant (R31). Data gains flatten beyond about 3.8M hours (R5, R6, R11, R12, R17, R18).
relationships.display_finding: The scaling curve requires an additive constant to capture saturation, and data gains flatten beyond about 3.8 million hours.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Wearable sensor pretraining; data and model scaling in the reported generative tasks
reader_labels.reason: Test error generally falls with more pretraining data and with larger models through LSM-Base in the tested ranges (R1-R4, R7-R10, R13-R16, R19-R21, R23-R25, R27-R29).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: High data scale and models larger than LSM-Base
reader_labels.reason: The 40 M-hour results do not improve on 6.6 M hours, and the 328M model is worse than the 110M model on the reported interpolation and extrapolation errors; the authors also report saturation (R5-R6, R11-R12, R17-R18, R22, R26, R30-R31).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuned exercise detection across the tested pretraining-data sizes
reader_labels.reason: Exercise detection accuracy and mAP increase across the reported data sizes (R32-R41).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Activity recognition accuracy and mAP are not monotonic across the full data sweep (R42-R51).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Compute and data scaling at the upper end of the tested ranges
reader_labels.reason: The authors report saturation at high compute, describe data-scaling gains as diminishing, and report no benefit from increasing the Base-model dataset from 6.6 M to 40 M hours (R5-R6, R11-R12, R17-R18, R31).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The study's broader setup-dependence and exponent claims
reader_labels.reason: The study shows saturation but does not compare fitting choices or establish that exponents differ across setups; its evidence supports only the curve-bending part of this version (R31).
